analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 income tax cuts, including lower rates on investment income, permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee with 31 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the scheduled expiration dates built into the 2001 and 2001-2003 tax laws, making every one of their provisions permanent: the across-the-board income tax rate cuts, the lower tax rates on dividends and capital gains, repeal of the estate tax, the child tax credit expansion, and more. It would also permanently extend three narrower provisions: the federal deduction for state and local sales taxes, the deduction for college tuition and related expenses, and an expanded write-off (up to $125,000, phasing out at $500,000 of investment) that lets businesses deduct equipment purchases immediately instead of depreciating them over years. Those tax laws were written with expiration dates, in part because their full permanent cost was large; this bill would remove that expiration.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest beneficiaries are high-income households and large estates, because making the 2001 and 2003 laws permanent locks in the lowest tax rates on capital gains and dividends, the top-rate cuts, and estate tax repeal indefinitely. Smaller benefits flow to small businesses that would keep the immediate $125,000 equipment write-off, to itemizers in states without an income tax who claim the sales-tax deduction, and to families claiming the tuition deduction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, estates, small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sunset provision of the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001, making all of its tax cuts permanent rather than expiring on schedule [S2][S3].
Makes permanent the reduced income tax rates on dividends and net capital gains enacted in 2003 [S2][S3].
Permanently extends the federal deduction for state and local sales taxes and the deduction for tuition and related expenses, both of which were otherwise set to lapse [S2][S3].

Makes permanent the expanded small-business expensing allowance of $125,000 (phasing out at $500,000 of qualifying investment, including computer software), with inflation adjustments after 2012 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury pays, through revenue forgone every year forever; the bill contains no offsetting tax increases or spending cuts. Because the largest permanent provisions (low investment-income rates and estate tax repeal) go overwhelmingly to high-income households and large estates, the cost of making up that revenue eventually falls on other taxpayers, on future spending, or on borrowing. Middle- and lower-income filers gain much less from the permanent provisions than high earners do.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal treasury and future taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill makes the tax cuts permanent without any offset, so every year of revenue forgone adds directly to federal deficits; the 2001 and 2003 laws were given expiration dates in part because their combined permanent cost was very large [S2][S3].

The permanent provisions are skewed toward the top of the income scale: the lowest tax rates apply to capital gains and dividends, income earned mainly by high-income households, and estate tax repeal benefits only the largest estates, while the benefits reaching ordinary filers (the sales-tax and tuition deductions) are comparatively small [S2].
Locking in the entire package permanently removes the flexibility that expiration dates gave Congress to revisit the tax code based on budget conditions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles genuinely useful middle-class provisions (permanent sales-tax and tuition deductions, a real small-business expensing break) into a package whose dominant component is making the entire 2001-2003 tax-cut framework permanent, with the largest and most permanent gains going to high-income households and large estates and no way to pay for any of it. An honest assessment: the middle-class pieces could stand on their own; the core of the bill is a permanent, unoffset transfer of tax reduction toward the top.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Randy Neugebauer introduced the bill on January 6, 2011, the first day of the 112th Congress [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
No further action of any kind — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — is recorded for the bill through the end of the 112th Congress [S5].
It attracted 31 cosponsors, all Republicans; no Democrat signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill itself, because it never advanced. Its death left the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts on their temporary footing, so the prospect of permanently locking in low investment-income rates and estate tax repeal ended for that Congress; anyone concerned about the unoffset revenue loss those permanence provisions would have caused is better off that it died.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the tax cuts stayed temporary

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee never moved it.

industries.note: Making the 2001 and 2003 laws permanent would lock in the lowest-ever tax rates on capital gains and dividends, income concentrated among high earners, and estate tax repeal for the largest estates. The cost is permanent revenue loss that must be made up by other taxpayers, future spending cuts, or borrowing.

A permanent $125,000 immediate write-off for equipment and software (phasing out at $500,000 of investment) lets profitable small firms deduct purchases up front instead of over years, improving cash flow. The benefit goes mainly to firms with profits large enough to shelter.

industries.industry: Itemizers in states without an income tax
industries.note: The permanent federal deduction for state and local sales taxes chiefly helps itemizing filers in states like Texas and Florida that have no income tax.
The deduction for tuition and related expenses, an expiring provision, would become permanent.
